title: Write a positioning statement and pass the competitor swap test
hypothesis: If we write a specific positioning statement and check it against the PDP, then strangers trust the account faster because the account and the product page say the same thing.
does_not_apply_when: an established account with a working feed and no stall

signal.check: The account has no clear one-line positioning, or a competitor's name could replace the brand's in the current bio or intro and still sound true.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources claim it builds trust but give no lift number

risk.note: Only changes wording; easy to revert if it does not read well.

prerequisites: a brand record with a real, verifiable proof point
steps: Fill in the template: I am X, I do Y for people who Z, listen because proof.
Pull the proof point from the brand record, not from guesswork.
Paste a direct competitor's name into the statement and check if it still reads true.
Tighten the audience or proof line until a competitor could not claim it.
Compare the statement to the PDP and collection page for a matching claim.
Store the statement where every hook and caption can be checked against it.

test.method: Compare the last 20 posts and hooks to the statement.
test.measure: share of hooks that trace back to the statement

title: Split unrelated product categories into separate content lines or accounts
hypothesis: If the account covers one product topic for one customer, then organic reach grows faster because ideas trace to one clear customer instead of scattered industry trends.
does_not_apply_when: a hero-SKU or single-category store

signal.check: The last 20 posts jump between unrelated product categories or customer types.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source gives the mechanism, not a lift number

risk.note: Splitting content lines is a planning change; merging back later is easy.

prerequisites: a catalogue that spans more than one clearly different customer or category
steps: List the last 20 posts and tag each by product category and customer.
Group categories that share one customer and one buying occasion.
Give each unrelated group its own content line, or its own account once a format has proven on the main account.
Draw new post ideas from that group's customer pain points, not industry trends.
Recheck the last 20 posts each month for topic consistency.

test.method: Run 4 weeks of split content lines and compare reach and saves per line to the mixed baseline month.
test.measure: organic_sessions and saves per content line
test.read_point: After 4 weeks at the new split

title: Pick 2 to 3 content pillars and map each to a product or collection
hypothesis: If the account runs 2 to 3 pillars from storytelling, ratings, breakdowns and scenarios, each tied to a product, then the feed builds a repeatable idea supply instead of one-off posts.

signal.check: The account has no named pillars, or storytelling is the only pillar running.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source gives a structure, not a measured lift

risk.note: Pillar choice is a planning decision and can change next month.

prerequisites: the account's positioning statement (ORG-001)
steps: List the 4 expert pillars: storytelling, ratings and rankings, breakdowns, scenarios.
Pick 2 pillars minimum, 3 if the team has capacity.
Map each pillar to a specific product or collection, not a generic 'our products' post.
If storytelling is chosen, pair it with at least one other pillar.
For a hero-SKU brand, run fewer pillars deeper on the one product; for a wide catalogue, rotate SKUs through the pillars.
Hold the chosen mix for a full month before changing it.

test.method: After 4 iterations per pillar, compare views, saves and comments by pillar.
test.read_point: After 4 posts per pillar, about 1 month

title: Choose expert or student on-camera stance based on what the brand can prove
hypothesis: If the on-camera person leads with real credentials only when the brand record backs them, and documents the journey as a student otherwise, then viewers trust the account because every expertise claim is provable.
does_not_apply_when: no credential and no willingness to document a learning journey on camera

signal.check: An on-camera person claims expertise or years of experience with nothing in the brand record to back it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; general practice, no lift measured

risk.note: An unbacked expertise claim can damage trust and invite public correction.

prerequisites: a documented list of real credentials, if any, in the brand record
steps: List every on-camera claim of expertise, years or test history.
Check each claim against the brand record.
Where a credential is real, lead with it and dress the part.
Where it is not, film the founder as a student trying and comparing options on camera.
For a considered or handmade product, favor the expert stance; for a commodity product, use the test-and-compare stance.

test.method: Compare comment sentiment and save rate between expert-framed and student-framed posts on the same product.

title: Write growth posts so a total stranger understands the product
hypothesis: If growth posts drop inside jokes, nicknames and assumed familiarity, then reach grows because most viewers of any post are new or infrequent, not existing followers.
does_not_apply_when: retention content aimed only at existing followers or customers

signal.check: Posts use product nicknames, collection names, size codes, or references to earlier videos, or follower share of views is above about 70%.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 4 presenters claim it but give no number

risk.note: A wording fix, easy to undo.

steps: Read the last 5 to 10 posts as if seeing the account for the first time.
Flag any nickname, SKU code, or reference to a past post.
Rewrite the opener to name the product plainly and lead with the clearest idea, not the cleverest.
Check the follower share of views after the next 5 posts.

test.method: Audit follower share of views before and after the rewrite.

title: Treat a broad viral hit with no buyer signal as a warning, not a win
hypothesis: If a post gets far more views than usual with no lift in saves, DMs or PDP visits, then the reach pulled in the wrong audience, because a broad hit gives the platform a noisy signal and rarely converts.
does_not_apply_when: a pure media or awareness account not selling a product

signal.check: A post's views spike well above baseline with no matching rise in saves, DMs or product page clicks.

expected_effect.size: unknown; qualitative claim only

risk.note: A read, not a change; low risk either way.

prerequisites: post-level views, saves, DM and PDP click data
steps: After any post far above baseline reach, pull saves, DMs and PDP clicks for it.
Compare them to the account's normal ratio of views to saves and DMs.
If the ratio is far below normal, treat the hit as noise, not a template to repeat.
Watch the next 3 posts to confirm reach held inside the buyer slice.

test.method: Track saves, DMs and PDP clicks per 1,000 views for the broad hit vs the account average.
test.measure: saves and DM rate per 1,000 views
test.read_point: Within a week of the broad hit

title: Turn a proven category post into a new one with the store's own angle
hypothesis: If the team takes a topic that already works in the category and adds the store's own method, material or segment, then new posts get a head start on structure while staying original, because blind copying gives random results.

signal.check: The idea bank is empty, or a competitor's post is being used as a direct model with no added angle.

expected_effect.size: unknown; general craft claim, no number

risk.note: Copying too closely risks brand and legal exposure; keep it to structure only.

prerequisites: a logged proven-topic research pass
steps: Research what already works in the category for this kind of post.
Name the store's missing perspective from the positioning statement: its method, material, segment or caveat.
Write the new post using only that gap, never the source's text, footage, product or faces.
Log both the proven topic and the store's angle side by side in the idea bank.

test.method: Compare completion and saves on the new angle post to the account's pillar average.

title: Put founder personality on the founder's account, not the brand handle
hypothesis: If personal biography and opinions run on a named founder or employee account and the brand account carries agreed positions and product content, then personality content performs better because a branded page underperforms a real person for it.
does_not_apply_when: faceless brands with no willing founder or employee

signal.check: Founder or employee personal stories are posted from the faceless brand handle instead of a named account.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source claims underperformance without a number

risk.note: An account-routing decision, easy to change.

prerequisites: a willing founder or named employee
steps: Decide who is front and centre: founder, employee or hired creator.
Route personal biography and opinion posts to that named person's account.
Keep agreed positions and standard product content on the brand account.
Batch filming with that same person so the account stays consistent.
Watch for fatigue if the same founder story repeats too often; rotate angles.

test.method: Compare engagement on personal-story posts from the named account vs the brand handle.
test.read_point: After 4 personal-story posts on each account

title: Test 3 reframes on the hero SKU before calling the category too boring for social
hypothesis: If a plain or functional product gets at least 3 pillar reframes and a single-visual-element test before anyone concludes the category cannot work, then the store finds a working angle because dullness is usually a treatment problem, not a category problem.

signal.check: The team says the product is too boring for social, or has stopped posting, with fewer than 3 reframed posts tried.

expected_effect.size: unknown; framed as strong personal conviction, not measured

risk.note: Only costs a few test posts.

prerequisites: the pillar list and idea bank
steps: Pick the hero SKU that feels hardest to make interesting.
Draft 3 different reframes from the pillar and angle menu.
Run the single distinctive visual element test on the first frame of each.
Ship all 3 and read completion and saves before making any verdict.
Only conclude the category does not work after all 3 have shipped and read.

test.method: Ship and compare 3 reframed posts against the account baseline.

title: Tag every post top, mid or bottom funnel and plan its reuse
hypothesis: If every post is tagged top, mid or bottom funnel before it is made and reused on the PDP, in email and in DMs, then views convert into sales more often because content stops asking for a sale on the first date.

signal.check: Posts get views but sales do not move, or the calendar has no funnel-stage column.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source frames the mechanism, not a lift number

risk.note: A tagging and planning change only.

prerequisites: a monthly calendar template
steps: Add a funnel-stage column to the calendar: top, mid or bottom.
Tag each planned post before it is scripted.
For top-funnel posts, aim for curiosity and trust only, no sale.
For mid-funnel posts, attach a guide, longer video or lead magnet.
For bottom-funnel posts, make the offer and confirm the PDP link and stock before it goes live.
Reuse each asset on the PDP, in a pre-purchase email and in a DM reply.

test.method: Check whether bottom-funnel posts have a live PDP link and whether sales move after they publish.

title: Label every post timely or timeless and strip dates from reusable content
hypothesis: If timeless posts carry no launch date or 'just launched' line, then they can be reused for years instead of decaying in about 24 hours like a timely post.

signal.check: A durable how-to, guide or origin-story post carries a date, a sale name or 'just launched' language.

expected_effect.size: unknown; general craft claim

risk.note: A labeling and editing step only.

steps: Add a timely or timeless label to every calendar entry.
For timeless posts, remove any date, sale name or 'just launched' line before publishing.
Keep real dates only on true stock and drop posts.
Ship any timely reaction to real news within 3 days or drop the idea.
Cap timely slots at 1 to 2 a week.

test.method: Track how many times each timeless post is reused across formats over a year.

title: Spend more production time only on posts with a long shelf life
hypothesis: If the team spends heavier production time only on pieces built to be reused for months, then the same hours produce more value because a quick restated tip does not deserve the same budget as a deep guide.

signal.check: A piece that would take much longer than a normal batch slot is being made with no plan to reuse it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; single-source example only

risk.note: A planning rule, no execution risk.

prerequisites: a written reuse plan for the piece
steps: Before starting any piece that would take longer than a normal batch slot, write its reuse list first.
If no reuse list exists, cut the piece back to a normal batch-slot post instead.
Reserve deep production time only for pieces with a written multi-surface reuse plan.

test.method: Compare hours spent per piece to the number of surfaces it later fed.
test.read_point: After the piece has been live a full quarter

title: Set starting cadence by catalogue shape: hero SKU vs wide catalogue
hypothesis: If a hero-SKU store runs 2 pillars on the one product and a wide catalogue rotates SKUs so none goes silent for a month, then the calendar matches the store's real catalogue shape instead of a generic plan.

signal.check: A new or restarted account has no calendar, or the current cadence ignores whether the store sells 1 hero product or many.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 presenter's coaching heuristic, no measured lift

risk.note: A calendar-planning change, easy to adjust.

prerequisites: the catalogue size and hero SKU status
steps: Confirm whether the store is hero-SKU or wide-catalogue.
For hero-SKU, run each chosen pillar twice a week on the one product.
For a wide catalogue, rotate SKUs through the pillars so none is silent for a month.
Set 4 to 6 posts a week as the default floor.
Hold the exact mix for one full month before changing it.
After about 4 iterations per pillar, read which pillar, topic, format and SKU pulls.

test.method: Compare pillar and SKU performance after 4 iterations each.
test.measure: views, saves, comments by pillar and SKU

title: Set a weekly posting floor the team can hold for 4 weeks straight
hypothesis: If the team sets a posting floor it can sustain for 4 weeks through order peaks, then content quality and consistency hold, because the floor is only raised once the monthly read shows the content works.

signal.check: The current posting plan cannot be held through a normal order peak, or posting has been irregular for more than 2 weeks.

expected_effect.size: sources disagree from about 1 to several posts a day; no single number is reliable

risk.note: A capacity-planning decision.

prerequisites: team capacity: on-camera people, editor hours, batch days
steps: List on-camera people, editor hours and batch days available each week.
Set the floor at the highest number the team can hold for 4 weeks, including a stock-out or peak week.
Do not judge content quality on posts made below this floor.
Raise the floor only after a monthly read shows the content works and unfollows or follower share did not worsen.

test.method: Track uploads shipped vs the floor for 4 weeks, then check unfollows and follower share.

title: Build a story and product-fact bank before buying more posting tools
hypothesis: If the team fills a bank of real stories and facts before adding a scheduler or new posting tool, then higher volume produces original posts instead of more generic 'premium quality' claims.

signal.check: The feed repeats generic claims like 'premium quality' with nothing behind them, while the team is shopping for a scheduler, editor or AI tool.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no number given

risk.note: A sequencing decision, not a spend.

steps: Pause any new posting-tool purchase.
Build the story and product-fact bank until it holds real material.
Only then evaluate a scheduler, editor tool or AI drafting tool.
Treat 'can we ship the volume' and 'do we have anything real to say' as 2 separate problems.

test.method: Count original, non-generic claims in the bank before approving a new tool purchase.

title: Batch scripting and filming on separate fixed days
hypothesis: If scripting happens on one fixed day and filming on a separate day, then the team ships more consistently because daily overthinking is what actually stops posting.
does_not_apply_when: accounts posting 3 or fewer times a week

signal.check: The account posts more than 3 times a week but scripts and films on the same day or with no fixed schedule.

expected_effect.size: unknown; workflow claim, no number

risk.note: A scheduling change only.

prerequisites: the idea bank and calendar
steps: Pick a fixed weekday for scripting only.
Write 3 to 5 scripts per sitting, continuing until 10 to 20 exist.
Pick a separate fixed day for filming all scripts back to back.
Keep research, writing and filming strictly separate; do not research on filming day.
Founder-led stores should aim to film about once every 2 weeks with scripts ready in advance.

test.method: Track weeks where the floor was hit vs missed before and after batching.

title: Hold the pillar mix 3 months and give the channel 12 months before a verdict
hypothesis: If the store holds its pillar mix for at least 3 months and does not judge the whole channel before 12 months of consistent posting, then real traction has time to show, because sources report from 1 to 12 months before results appear.
does_not_apply_when: a gap month with no posts, which resets the clock

signal.check: An owner asks whether organic is working after only a few weeks of posting.

expected_effect.size: 1 to 12 months depending on source; strictest kept is 12 months

risk.note: A patience rule, not an action with downside.

prerequisites: consistent posting at the floor for the whole window
steps: Set the review calendar to check the pillar mix no sooner than 3 months in.
Set the channel-level verdict date to 12 months from the first consistent posting month.
If a gap month happens, such as a stock-out with no posts, reset the clock.
Track uploads vs floor throughout, not views or sales, until the first macro read.

test.method: Compare organic sessions and saves at month 3, 6 and 12 against the starting baseline.

title: Track posts shipped against the floor as the only KPI for months 1 to 3
hypothesis: If the team tracks only posts shipped vs the floor in months 1 to 3, then the account avoids stalling from watching a follower count the team cannot yet control.
does_not_apply_when: an account with more than 3 months of consistent posting history

signal.check: A new account's weekly report leads with views, followers or sales instead of posts shipped vs floor.

expected_effect.size: unknown; input-metric framing, not a lift

risk.note: A reporting change only.

steps: Add a weekly line to the experiment log: planned, shipped, missed.
Report only this line to the founder for the first 3 months.
Hold off on any strategy change based on views or follower count in this window.

test.method: Review the weekly planned-vs-shipped log.

title: Stop comparing the account's growth to bigger brands or established creators
hypothesis: If review meetings never open with a competitor's follower count, then the team avoids the 'why not me' stall that comparisons against much bigger accounts create.

signal.check: A review meeting opens by comparing the store's follower count or growth speed to a bigger brand or creator.

expected_effect.size: unknown; behavioural claim, not measured

risk.note: A reporting habit change.

steps: Remove any slide or dashboard line ranking the account against another brand's followers.
Use other accounts only for format ideas and category gaps.
Replace outside benchmarks with the store's own trend over time.

test.method: Check whether the next review meeting cites an outside follower count.
test.measure: presence of outside benchmarks in the readout

title: Turn the questions under your best posts into new posts from month 2
hypothesis: If the team opens a post with the exact question buyers keep asking in comments and answers it with the product in hand, then the idea bank never runs dry and content matches real buyer doubt.
does_not_apply_when: accounts with fewer than 4 weeks of comments to mine

signal.check: A month of comments on product posts repeats the same questions about fit, care or price with no post answering them directly.

expected_effect.size: unknown; process claim, no lift given

risk.note: Content planning only.

prerequisites: at least a month of comments on prior posts
steps: Pull the repeated questions from the last month of comments.
Pick one question a week starting month 2.
Open the post with the exact question, then answer it with the product in hand.
Also answer the questions buyers are embarrassed to ask directly.

test.method: Compare completion and saves on comment-question posts to the pillar average.

title: Delay posting-time, audio and repost tricks until the story bank and floor exist
hypothesis: If the team ignores posting-time, trending-audio and repost tricks until the story bank and posting floor are in place, then effort goes to what moves the account instead of micro-tactics with no library behind them.
does_not_apply_when: accounts that already hold a full story bank and a met floor

signal.check: A team debates posting time, trending audio or repost tricks while the feed is still under the posting floor.

expected_effect.size: unknown; framed as a distraction to avoid, not a lift

risk.note: A prioritisation rule only.

steps: Confirm the story bank and posting floor are in place first.
Log any micro-tactic idea (posting time, trending audio, close-friends trick) in the experiment log instead of acting on it.
Test micro-tactics only after the floor and bank are met.

test.method: Compare reach on posts made with and without micro-tactic changes once the floor and bank exist.
test.read_point: After the floor and bank are in place for 4 weeks

title: Keep a permanent bank of 10 to 20 one-line post ideas, each naming a SKU
hypothesis: If the idea bank never drops below 10 lines, each naming a proven topic, the store's angle and a SKU, then batch days never stall for lack of a script to write.

signal.check: A batch day is approaching and the scripts folder or idea bank has fewer than 10 lines.

expected_effect.size: unknown; workflow rule, no lift given

risk.note: A maintenance habit only.

prerequisites: the competitive research log (see idea-bank research idea)
steps: Check the idea bank count before every batch day.
Draw new lines from research and comments, not memory.
Refill to at least 10 lines before scripting starts.
Tag each line with a SKU.

test.method: Track idea bank count over time and whether batch days ever start below 10 lines.

title: Do not abandon the account after a run of weak posts
hypothesis: If the team runs the last-20-post audit and follower-share check before restarting an account after a flat quarter, then a real strategy problem is separated from normal post-to-post variance.

signal.check: An owner wants to start fresh or abandon the account after a flat quarter of weak posts.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the claim overstates variance per its own source note

risk.note: A decision check, not an action with downside.

steps: Before any restart decision, run the last-20-video topic and avatar audit.
Run the follower-share-of-views check.
Only restart the account if both checks point to a real strategy problem, not normal variance.

test.method: Compare the next 4 posts after applying the audits to the prior flat quarter.

title: Confirm stock, shipping and reply capacity before a post is built to pull orders
hypothesis: If units on hand, ship time and who answers DMs are confirmed before a lead magnet or selling post goes live, then a viral spike does not overwhelm a thin-stock SKU or an unstaffed inbox.
does_not_apply_when: a deep-stock SKU with an existing waitlist path

signal.check: A lead magnet or DM automation is about to go live, or a thin-stock hero SKU is about to get a selling post, with no stated units on hand.

expected_effect.size: unknown; general practice example, no measured lift

risk.note: A stockout or unanswered DM spike from an unchecked post cannot be undone after it happens.

prerequisites: current units on hand and DM reply capacity
steps: Check units on hand for the featured SKU before the post goes live.
Confirm ship time and who answers DMs and comments that day.
If the post could sell more than the team can fulfil, set up the waitlist path first.
Record units, ship time and the DM owner on the calendar row.

test.method: Compare orders and DM volume from the post to stock on hand and reply capacity.

title: Rotate which SKU gets a post so no item goes untouched for a month
hypothesis: If a wide catalogue rotates which SKU gets a post, weighted toward margin and stock depth, then no product goes silent for a month and slow movers get a chance at demand.
does_not_apply_when: a single hero-SKU brand, which deepens angles on one product instead

signal.check: A catalogue of 50 or more items has a feed that keeps returning to the same 3 products.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data

risk.note: A calendar planning change only.

prerequisites: a SKU list with margin and stock depth
steps: List all SKUs with margin and current stock depth.
Build a rotation plan weighted toward margin and stock depth.
Add the SKU column to the calendar and check coverage each month.
Flag any SKU untouched for a month and schedule it next.

test.method: Count distinct SKUs featured per month against total catalogue size.

title: Spend most hook-planning time on the first 3 seconds
hypothesis: If most planning time and effort goes to the first 3 seconds of every video, then more viewers stay past the hook because the hook decides whether the product is seen at all.

signal.check: The 3-second watch rate per post is low or has not been tracked.

expected_effect.size: unknown; presenter heuristic (80% of planning time), no lift given

risk.note: A time-allocation change only.

steps: Track the 3-second watch rate per post, split by SKU.
Reallocate script time so the hook and first frame get the majority of planning effort.
Review the hook checklist before moving on to the rest of the script.

test.method: Compare 3-second watch rate before and after shifting planning time.

title: Plan the first frame around the product before writing the hook line
hypothesis: If the first frame shows the product as a prop, a face, movement or an unusual vantage point instead of a logo or static packshot, then fewer viewers swipe before the hook line is read.

signal.check: The first frame of a video or carousel shows a logo, a static packshot, or the founder at a desk with no product visible.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no number given

risk.note: A shot-planning change.

steps: Write down the visual event before the hook line: a prop in hand, a face to camera, movement, a lighting change, or an unusual vantage point.
Screenshot the video at about half a second and check a stranger can name the product type.
Reshoot or recut any opener where the first frame is generic or unrelated to the product.

test.method: Run the half-second screenshot test on the next 5 videos before publishing.
test.measure: pass rate on the screenshot test

title: Keep the on-screen hook line to 5 to 8 words
hypothesis: If the on-screen hook line stays at 5 to 8 words and rarely goes above 12, then more viewers process it before swiping, because a self-collected sample of 1,300 Reels found top performers averaged 7.7 words.

signal.check: Hook text wraps to 3 lines over the product shot, or word count has never been checked.

expected_effect.size: top performers averaged 7.7 words in a self-collected, undisclosed-method sample

risk.note: A text-editing rule only.

steps: Count words in the on-screen and spoken hook line.
Cut to 5 to 8 words, up to about 12 at most.
Move any extra detail into the caption, which can run longer.

test.method: Compare hook_rate on posts under 8 words vs longer hooks.
test.read_point: After 10 posts logged with word counts

title: Cap hook and body reading grade below tenth grade, matched to the PDP
hypothesis: If the hook stays at or below 5th grade and body copy at 5th to 8th grade, matched to the PDP and checkout copy, then a viewer who clicks through meets the same voice and does not stall on unfamiliar words.

signal.check: A hook, script or caption scores above the store's PDP copy, or above 10th grade on a readability check.

expected_effect.size: unknown; readability targets are craft standards, not measured lifts

risk.note: An editing pass only.

prerequisites: a readability tool
steps: Run every hook and caption through a readability checker.
Cap hooks at 5th grade and body copy at 5th to 8th grade, never above 10th.
Check the PDP and checkout copy's reading grade and match it.
Replace multi-syllable and niche words that push the score up.

test.method: Compare reading grade scores before and after the pass across a batch of posts.

title: Run the drunk grandma test: cut jargon a stranger would not understand
hypothesis: If every hook is read by an outsider with zero context, then hooks that use trade terms, material codes or acronyms get cut, because a stranger must understand the product and the point instantly to keep watching.

signal.check: A hook uses trade terms, material codes, collection names or acronyms an outsider would not know.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no number given

risk.note: A wording check only.

steps: Read the hook and first frame with zero context, as a stranger would.
Cut insider terms, acronyms and unexplained jargon.
Confirm an outsider can name the product and the point from the hook alone.

test.method: Ask someone outside the team to explain the hook after one viewing.
test.measure: pass rate on the outsider test

title: Open hooks with the before-state and hold the payoff for later
hypothesis: If a story or curiosity hook opens with the before-state, names the stakes and withholds the specific result until the payoff, then more viewers stay because the gap is neither too wide nor too narrow.
does_not_apply_when: direct-benefit hooks for bottom-funnel or Story CTAs

signal.check: A hook already gives the mechanism or the result, or is so vague the viewer cannot tell the product or the stakes.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim shared across 4 sources, no measured lift

risk.note: A gap with no real payoff reads as bait and can hurt trust; the payoff must be genuine.

steps: Open the hook with the product's before-state: the tangled chain, the pan that sticks.
Name what is at risk without revealing the outcome.
Withhold the specific result until the payoff later in the piece.
Confirm the payoff actually appears and matches the brand record before publishing.

test.method: Track retention through the middle of the video against hooks that reveal everything up front.

title: Test a warning-style hook against a benefit hook on the same product
hypothesis: If both a negative-framed and positive-framed version of the same hook are logged and tested, then the account learns which framing this audience responds to instead of assuming either wins.
does_not_apply_when: a warm or luxury voice that excludes threat language

signal.check: The hooks bank has only benefit hooks, or only warning-style hooks, with no comparison logged.

expected_effect.size: one presenter's self-collected sample found threat-word hooks outperformed on average

risk.note: Both versions stay inside the brand voice; drop the negative version if it does not fit.

prerequisites: the brand voice rules on allowed tone
steps: Write a negative-framed and a positive-framed version of the same hook line.
Check both fit inside the brand's voice; drop the one that does not.
Publish or test both and log which framing was used per post.
Read results monthly by framing type.

test.method: Compare hook_rate between negative-framed and positive-framed posts over a month.

title: Pick the hook type on purpose from a 15-type menu and log it
hypothesis: If every hook is chosen on purpose from a menu of 15 types and tagged in the hooks bank, then the account stops defaulting to one habitual type and can read which types actually work.

signal.check: The hooks bank shows one hook type dominating the last 5 or more posts.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a structural claim, not a measured lift

risk.note: A tagging and variety rule only.

prerequisites: the 15 hook types listed in the hooks bank template
steps: List the last 5 hook types used.
Pick a different type from the 15-type menu for the next hook.
For outcome or authority hooks, cite only a real result or figure from the brand record.
Log the hook type in the hooks bank once the post is scripted.

test.method: Track hook type distribution and performance monthly.

title: Prefer a friend-style hook with a real payoff over a loud formula
hypothesis: If a hook that sounds like a friend's tip still names a concrete payoff, it can outperform recognised bait formulas like '3 mistakes you're making', because audiences discount formulas they recognise as ads.

signal.check: The hooks bank is full of '3 mistakes' and 'stop doing this' formula openers with no conversational alternative logged.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 presenter's example vs another presenter's opposite finding

risk.note: Keep both versions in the bank; let the monthly read decide.

steps: Draft the formula version of the hook.
Rewrite it as a friend would say it, keeping the same concrete payoff.
Read both aloud and keep the one that still sounds like a friend, not an ad.
Log both versions and let the monthly read decide which type wins.

test.method: Compare hook_rate between formula-style and conversational-style hooks over a month.

title: Only run a hook swap with a matched cut and confirmed rights
hypothesis: If a hook swap only runs when the last frame of the borrowed clip matches the first frame of the store's footage in motion or composition, and rights are confirmed, then the swap keeps viewers without legal exposure.
does_not_apply_when: no confirmed usage rights on the borrowed clip

signal.check: A plan to open with a borrowed viral clip or staged dramatic moment exists with no rights check or no genuine match point.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no number given

risk.note: An unlicensed clip can bring takedown or legal risk once published.

prerequisites: confirmed usage rights on the borrowed clip
steps: Find a genuine match point between the borrowed clip's last frame and the store's own footage.
If there is no real match, do not force the transition; pick a different hook type instead.
Confirm usage rights in writing before editing.
File the rights confirmation before the edit goes to production.

test.method: Track hook_rate on rights-confirmed hook-swap posts vs the account baseline.

title: Cut dead time from the first second of every video
hypothesis: If the product or the problem is visible at half a second, with no pause, static shot or clutter, then fewer viewers swipe away before the hook starts.

signal.check: A video opens with a pause, a static packshot, visual clutter or low contrast.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no number given

risk.note: An editing cut only.

steps: Cut any pause, setup shot or clutter from the first second.
Screenshot at about half a second and check a stranger can say what product it is.
Recut if the frame is ambiguous or low contrast.

test.method: Compare 3-second watch rate before and after removing dead time.

title: Use only specific product numbers the brand record can back
hypothesis: If outcome and data-backed hooks use realistic, backed numbers instead of extreme or invented ones, then hooks hold credibility and avoid a false-claim risk.

signal.check: An outcome or data-backed hook cites a number, study or comparison not in the brand's claims list.

expected_effect.size: realistic figures held more viewers than extreme ones in one presenter's account

risk.note: An uncited number risks a false-claim complaint if it reaches enough viewers.

prerequisites: the brand's substantiated claims list
steps: Compare every number in an outcome or data-backed hook to the claims list.
Remove or replace any number the brand record cannot support.
Prefer a realistic, specific figure over an extreme one when both are true.

test.method: Audit hooks for unbacked numbers before every publish.

title: Only cite a named, real lab, standard or body in authority hooks
hypothesis: If an authority hook names a real, checkable lab, standard or body, then stranger scepticism drops, because a citation only works if it is true and the certificate or report exists.

signal.check: An authority hook says 'lab tested' or 'certified' with no named, verifiable source.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: An uncited authority claim risks false-advertising exposure.

prerequisites: the substantiated claims list with named certifications
steps: Check that any 'lab tested' or 'certified' line names a real body.
Confirm the citation exists in the substantiated claims list.
Cut the line if the certificate or report cannot be produced on request.

test.method: Audit authority hooks against the claims list before publishing.

title: Run contrarian and bold-claim hooks only on positions the brand will defend
hypothesis: If contrarian and bold-claim hooks only run on positions the store actually holds and will defend in the comments, then the hook builds a distinct voice instead of manufactured controversy that undermines credibility.
does_not_apply_when: luxury or regulated brands outside a lower-stakes test account

signal.check: A hot-take or contrarian hook is drafted about a position the brand has not actually taken or will not defend publicly.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a hedged verdict is said to undermine credibility faster than a boring post

risk.note: A position the brand will not defend in public can backfire in the comments.

prerequisites: a positions log recording the brand's side on category debates
steps: Check the positions log for the brand's real stance on the topic.
Confirm the owner will answer comments that challenge the position.
Route the hook through the compliance check if it names a competitor or a health or safety claim.
Publish only after both checks pass.

test.method: Track comment sentiment and reply volume on contrarian posts.

title: Write identity hooks around buyer behaviour, never a judgment on who they are
hypothesis: If identity hooks describe what the buyer does instead of judging who they are, then the hook works through self-comparison instead of risking a stereotyping backlash.

signal.check: An identity or direct-address hook carries a judgmental label instead of a behaviour description.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a risk-avoidance claim, not a measured lift

risk.note: A judgmental or stereotyping label can draw public backlash once published.

steps: Read the identity hook line and identify whether it judges the buyer or describes their behaviour.
Rewrite any judgmental phrase ('lazy parents feed their kids like this') around behaviour ('serious home cooks never do this').
Check the rewrite still names a concrete moment the buyer would recognise.

test.method: Run every identity hook past the pre-publish checklist for judgmental language.
test.measure: pass rate on the identity-language check

title: Deliver the full count promised in every list hook
hypothesis: If a list hook like '3 ways to wear it' delivers all 3 with the product shown for each, then retention holds, because a broken count breaks the implicit promise.

signal.check: A list hook promises a count and the body delivers fewer items.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no number given

risk.note: A script-editing check only.

steps: Count the items promised in the hook.
Confirm the script shows the product for each promised item.
Cut the promised count in the hook if the script cannot deliver it.

test.method: Compare hold_rate on list posts that deliver the full count vs those that fall short.

title: Make every hook work on mute with text and visual alone
hypothesis: If the first 3 seconds work with the sound off, then fewer viewers are lost, because a large share of viewers watch on mute and a loud effect alone cannot carry the hook.

signal.check: A hook relies on a sound effect or spoken line with no supporting on-screen text or visual.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no number given

risk.note: An editing check only.

steps: Watch the first 3 seconds on mute.
Confirm the hook still lands from text and visual alone.
Add on-screen text or a stronger visual interrupt if the hook depends on sound.

test.method: Watch every video on mute before publishing.
test.measure: pass rate on the mute test

title: Open dry product topics with the scene the buyer already cares about
hypothesis: If a dry product topic (thread count, alloy, wattage) opens with a scenario the buyer already likes, then more strangers watch, because the mechanism only lands once the scenario has earned attention.

signal.check: A post about a technical or dry product spec has never used a scenario opener.

expected_effect.size: unknown; general practice example, verify against brand data

risk.note: Pop-culture or news-based scenarios need a defamation and endorsement screen before shipping.

steps: Identify the dry technical topic to be covered.
Find a scene or reference the buyer already knows and likes.
Open with the scenario, then bring in the product mechanism inside it.
Screen any reference to real people, brands or news for defamation and endorsement risk.
Ship within 3 days if the reference is timely, or drop it.

test.method: Compare completion rate on scenario-first openers vs spec-first openers on similar topics.

title: Make relatable hooks specific to a real buyer moment with the product
hypothesis: If relatable, POV and scenario hooks name a concrete moment the buyer has actually been in, then the hook lands with fewer but more resonant viewers than a vague version of the same idea.

signal.check: A relatable or POV hook is generic ('me when my order is late') instead of a specific, vivid moment.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no number given

risk.note: A wording rewrite only.

steps: Draft the generic version of the relatable moment.
Add a specific, vivid detail the buyer has actually experienced.
Check the moment assumes the viewer already owns or wants a similar product.

test.method: Compare saves and comments on specific vs generic relatable hooks.

title: Sharpen flat copy with the most charged true wording, not exaggeration
hypothesis: If a flat script is sharpened to its most specific, most charged true wording instead of an exaggerated AI rewrite, then the copy gets stronger without inventing a claim the brand cannot back.

signal.check: A script or caption reads flat and a writer is tempted to inflate it with an AI-generated exaggerated version.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this replaces a risky source practice with a safer one, no lift claimed

risk.note: A wording discipline, replacing a riskier practice.

prerequisites: the substantiated claims list
steps: Identify the flat line that needs more charge.
List the true, specific details behind it from the brand record.
Choose the most charged true wording that still matches those facts exactly.
Never ask an AI tool for an 'exaggerated' version; ask for the 'most specific, most concrete true wording' instead.

test.method: Compare engagement on the charged-true version vs the original flat line.

title: Name the reaction, action and one-line takeaway before writing any script
hypothesis: If every script starts by naming the intended emotion, the buyer's action and the one line to remember, then the finished piece stays focused because the outline is replaced by a single fixed thesis.

signal.check: A writer starts a script or caption with a blank page and no stated emotion, action or takeaway.

expected_effect.size: unknown; process claim, no lift given

risk.note: A writing process step only.

steps: Name the intended reaction: awe, outrage, warmth or curiosity.
Name the action: comment the keyword, save, share or buy.
Write the one line the buyer should remember, replacing the outline.
Write these 3 decisions at the top of the script before drafting starts.

test.method: Check whether the finished piece delivers the stated one-line takeaway.
test.measure: presence of a clear one-line takeaway

title: Put the product promise first and cut the background from every opener
hypothesis: If a caption opens with the product promise or the most provocative true line instead of the brand's history, then more readers stay past the first sentence, because context belongs after the reader is invested.

signal.check: A caption opens with 'we're excited to announce' or the brand's backstory instead of the thesis.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: An editing rule only.

steps: Read only the first sentence of the caption.
Delete it unless it is the thesis, promise or most provocative true statement.
Move context to about sentence 3 or 4, after the reader is invested.

test.method: Compare read-through and save rates on rewritten openers vs the prior style.
test.read_point: After the next batch of captions

title: Run a readability pass to cut jargon, adverbs and thesaurus words
hypothesis: If every script and caption is edited to cut adverbs, trade jargon and thesaurus words before publishing, then more readers finish and understand the copy, because a word the customer would not say gets cut.

signal.check: Copy scores above the target reading grade, or contains words a customer would not use in conversation.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim from outside retail, not a store benchmark

risk.note: An editing pass only.

steps: Read the draft and flag any word that needed a dictionary check.
Flag any word the customer would not say about the product.
Cut or replace flagged words.
Rerun the readability check to confirm the grade target is met.

test.method: Compare reading grade and completion rate before and after the pass.

title: Write every caption to one named customer, not to 'our community'
hypothesis: If every caption is written to one real or composite buyer instead of 'our community', then copy stops sounding like a press release and reads as a direct message someone can act on.

signal.check: A caption reads corporate or addresses 'everyone' or 'our community' instead of one buyer.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: A rewriting rule only.

prerequisites: the single customer avatar from the account foundations
steps: Pick one real or composite buyer from the brand record.
Rewrite the caption to speak only to that one person.
Check the caption no longer sounds like a press release.

test.method: Compare comments and DM replies on avatar-targeted captions vs 'community' captions.

title: Cut stacked synonyms in every script
hypothesis: If a script's stacked synonyms ('soft, cosy, comfortable, snug') are cut to the one word that says it, then viewers stay instead of scrolling past repeated filler.

signal.check: A script stacks 2 or more adjectives that repeat the same idea about the product.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: An editing pass only.

steps: Read each sentence and ask 'necessary, or already said?'
Cut every adjective that repeats a point already made.
Keep only the strongest single word for the idea.

test.method: Compare hold_rate on edited scripts vs the prior draft style.

title: Drop school-style padding and formal outlines from product captions
hypothesis: If captions drop padded length, fancy words and formal outlines in favour of a single one-line thesis, then copy reads faster and closer to how the customer actually talks.
does_not_apply_when: PDP and blog copy that needs SEO depth, which this rule does not override

signal.check: A caption is padded to 'look complete' or follows a brand-outline template with no clear one-line thesis.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: An editing rule only.

steps: Identify the one-line thesis for the caption.
Cut any sentence that only pads length or restates the outline.
Keep captions short unless the platform or format needs more detail.

test.method: Compare completion and save rates on shortened captions vs the padded style.
test.read_point: After the next batch of captions

title: Say the product topic and the buyer out loud in the video and caption
hypothesis: If every video names the product type and who it is for, both in speech and in the caption, then the account builds a clearer topic signal and any comment keyword lands with the right context.

signal.check: A video never speaks the product category out loud, or the caption is only hashtags with no topic or audience line.

expected_effect.size: unknown; presented as a claim about topic learning, not measured

risk.note: A scripting and caption habit only.

steps: Add a spoken line naming the product type and who it is for.
Repeat the same naming in the caption's first line.
If a comment keyword is used, put it on screen and in the caption too.

test.method: Audit the last 20 videos for a spoken topic and audience line.
test.measure: share of posts naming topic and audience

title: Let humans originate stories and positions; use AI only to remix approved lines
hypothesis: If AI only remixes sentences a human has already approved, and humans always originate new stories or positions, then AI-assisted content stays true to the brand instead of drifting into generic claims.

signal.check: An AI-assisted piece states a new position, a first-told story or a specific customer story with no human origin tagged.

expected_effect.size: unknown; process rule, no lift given

risk.note: An AI-originated claim that turns out false can damage trust before it is caught.

prerequisites: a positions log and an approved story set
steps: Decide per piece whether it is 'originated by [name]' or 'remix' before drafting.
Route any net-new position, first-told story or specific customer story to a human writer.
Use AI only to slice, cross-format or generate variations of already-approved lines.
Tag every AI-assisted piece with its mode before publishing.

test.method: Audit a sample of AI-assisted posts each month for untagged or misclassified pieces.

title: Keep a positions log of the brand's side on category debates
hypothesis: If the brand's side on recurring category debates (material vs synthetic, price vs quality, in-house vs sourced) is written down before any AI draft, then AI-assisted copy says something a competitor could not say.

signal.check: An AI draft reads as generic copy any competitor in the category could post.

expected_effect.size: unknown; single-source claim, no lift given

risk.note: A documentation task, low risk.

prerequisites: the category's recurring debates identified
steps: List the category's recurring debates that gate a purchase decision.
Write the brand's real position on each, or mark it 'deliberately neutral'.
Store the positions log in the brand record for writers and AI to reference.
Check every AI draft against the log before it ships.

test.method: Compare AI drafts written with and without the positions log for genericness.
test.measure: share of drafts flagged as generic in review

title: Rewrite prescriptive advice as first-person product experience
hypothesis: If prescriptive lines ('you should season your pan monthly') are rewritten as a first-person product test ('I used this for 30 days before we shipped it'), then the copy reads as personality instead of commodity advice.
does_not_apply_when: benefit-focused 'you' lines, which are standard converting copy and stay as is

signal.check: A draft contains prescriptive 'you should' advice that any competitor in the category could also say.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: A rewrite only.

steps: Find prescriptive 'you should' lines in the draft.
Rewrite each as a specific first-person product test or experience.
Leave benefit 'you' lines ('you'll get X') untouched.
Route the first-person version to the named person's account.

test.method: Compare engagement on rewritten first-person lines vs the original prescriptive version.
test.read_point: After the next batch of posts

title: Fix the one off voice variable instead of rewriting a whole draft
hypothesis: If a voice complaint on an AI or ghostwritten draft is fixed by adjusting the one off variable (word register, sentence length, opinion vs citation) instead of the whole piece, then the fix is small and the voice guide improves.

signal.check: A draft 'doesn't sound like the brand' and the team is about to rewrite it from scratch.

expected_effect.size: one presenter's case fixed a complaint with a 1% edit (2 to 3 citation phrases)

risk.note: A small edit, easy to revert.

prerequisites: the brand's voice variables: register, rhythm, stance
steps: Identify which of the 3 voice variables is off: word register, sentence rhythm, or opinion vs citation stance.
Make the smallest edit on that one variable.
Record the confirmed fix in the brand voice guide for next time.

test.method: Re-read the edited draft against the voice complaint.
test.measure: pass or fail on the voice check

title: Build the story set: founder history, sourcing trips, failed batches, positions
hypothesis: If founder history, sourcing trips, failed batches and product positions are stored where writers and AI can read them, then generic claims like 'we care about quality' get replaced with a specific true story.

signal.check: Captions repeat 'we care about quality' or similar generic claims with nothing specific behind them.

expected_effect.size: unknown; general practice example, verify against brand data

risk.note: A documentation task.

prerequisites: founder history and permission to use real stories
steps: Interview the founder for real history, failures and sourcing stories.
Store each story with a topic, emotion and format label.
Mark each story approved once it has been told well once or twice.
Drop the specific story into the exact slot where a generic claim would go.
Build this before scaling posting volume.

test.method: Track the share of posts using an approved specific story vs a generic claim.
test.read_point: Monthly AI draft and content review

title: Use AI as a pre-publish reviewer with targeted questions, not an open prompt
hypothesis: If a script or caption is reviewed with 4 targeted AI questions about hook clarity, buyer understanding, phone readability and drop-off points, then edits catch more real problems than an open-ended AI request would.

signal.check: A script is ready to film or a caption ready to post with no targeted AI review pass done.

expected_effect.size: unknown; process claim, no lift given

risk.note: A review step; a human still applies edits by hand.

steps: Paste the script or caption into the AI tool.
Ask: is the hook clear in under 3 seconds?
Ask: would a first-time buyer immediately understand what this is about?
Ask: make this shorter and easier to read on a phone.
Ask: where could I cut so viewers do not drop off?
Apply the suggested edits by hand and fact-check any claim against the brand record.

test.method: Compare hook_rate on AI-reviewed scripts vs unreviewed scripts.
test.read_point: After the next batch of scripts

title: Check every AI-remixed piece for facts and voice before it goes live
hypothesis: If a human signs off on every AI-remixed piece's material, price, guarantee, delivery time or result claims, then AI repeating a false claim never reaches a customer, because AI repeats, it does not verify.

signal.check: An AI remix names a material, price, guarantee, delivery time or result with no human fact check logged.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a checkpoint rule, no lift given

risk.note: A missed false claim can reach customers before it is caught.

prerequisites: the brand record and PDP as the source of truth
steps: List every factual claim in the AI-remixed piece.
Check each one against the brand record and the PDP.
Get a human sign-off before publishing.
Log the check in the piece's compliance record.

test.method: Audit a sample of published AI-remixed pieces monthly for unflagged errors.

title: Publish small posts to find the founder's voice instead of waiting to feel ready
hypothesis: If a founder-led account ships 4 short posts and compares variants instead of waiting for the voice to feel ready, then the account moves past the stall, because 'I don't like my voice' is usually a fear problem, not a voice problem.

signal.check: A founder-led account is stalled saying 'we haven't found our tone' with fewer than 4 short posts shipped.

expected_effect.size: unknown; process claim, no lift given

risk.note: Low-stakes plain opinions are low risk to publish.

steps: Pick 4 low-risk, plain-opinion post ideas.
Ship all 4 without a voice workshop first.
Compare which variants felt most natural and performed best.
Record the confirmed voice choices for future scripts.

test.method: Compare engagement across the 4 shipped variants.

title: Ask each month whether an AI-drafted piece added something new or only rearranged
hypothesis: If the monthly read tracks whether each AI-drafted piece added something new about the product or only rearranged old material, then the story set grows instead of cycling the same few claims.

signal.check: The monthly read has no count of originated vs remixed pieces.

expected_effect.size: unknown; tracking claim, no lift given

risk.note: A tracking addition only.

prerequisites: the AI mode tag on each piece
steps: Pull every AI-drafted piece from the month.
Mark each as net-new or a rearrangement of existing material.
Add the count to the monthly performance read.
Flag months where the remix share is rising and the story set is not growing.

test.method: Track the ratio of originated to remixed pieces over 3 months.

title: Lead product content with sensory in-use footage; move specs to the body or PDP
hypothesis: If the first 10 seconds show the product in use or in a story instead of a spec list, then more viewers stay, because a story of someone using the product engages differently than a fact list.

signal.check: A PDP or script opens with a feature or spec list above the fold instead of the product in use.

expected_effect.size: one presenter's own case broke a 400,000-view ceiling after switching to story-first; not independently measured

risk.note: A script-structure change only.

steps: Identify posts and PDP sections that open with specs.
Rewrite the first 10 seconds or first paragraph as the product in use or a short story.
Move the spec list to the body or a dedicated PDP section.
Check the story or use-case still names the product plainly.

test.method: Compare hold_rate and PDP time-on-page for story-first vs spec-first versions.

title: Mine product stories with a fixed question set when the idea bank runs low
hypothesis: If the team answers a fixed set of story questions (what buyers wrongly believe, what is controversial, the most inspiring customer story, proof against competitors, the strangest fact, recent category news) per hero SKU, then the idea bank refills with real material instead of running dry.

signal.check: The idea bank has fewer than 10 lines.

expected_effect.size: unknown; process claim, no lift given

risk.note: A research exercise only.

prerequisites: founder and customer story access
steps: Ask: what does everyone think is true about the product but isn't?
Ask: what is controversial or frustrating in the category?
Ask: what is the most inspiring customer story, with permission to film it?
Ask: what proves the product beats competitors, as a story not a chart?
Ask: what is the strangest or most visually shocking thing about it?
Ask: what happened in the category's news in the last 3 days?
Log the 6 answers per hero SKU in the story bank.

test.method: Count new idea bank lines added after the exercise.

title: Name what the founder or customer wanted and what stood in the way, fast
hypothesis: If every story names the want and the obstacle early, then viewers do not lose the thread, because a story that wanders past the first few seconds loses the audience.

signal.check: A story draft wanders without a clear stated want or obstacle in the first few sentences.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: A script structure check only.

steps: Pause anywhere in the draft and ask what the person wants and what is in the way.
If either cannot be named instantly, move it earlier in the script.
Check both are visible in the first 3 sentences.

test.method: Run the pause test on the finished draft before filming.
test.measure: pass or fail on the pause test

title: Build a 30-minute founder-history carousel for a same-day calendar gap
hypothesis: If the team builds a founder-history carousel (1 iconic event per year, including failures, with photos and text overlays) in 30 minutes, then a calendar gap gets filled with a real story instead of a generic filler post.

signal.check: A calendar gap needs a post today and the founder has a real timeline to draw from.

expected_effect.size: one presenter reports 45,000 likes on his own attempt; a self-reported single example

risk.note: A quick production task with low risk.

prerequisites: the founder's real timeline and photos, confirmed for accuracy
steps: Write down the last 10 to 20 years of the business, 1 iconic event per year, including failed products and bad seasons.
Pick 1 photo per moment.
Add a short text overlay per photo.
Confirm every event and date with the founder before posting.
Assemble and post the carousel.

test.method: Compare likes and saves on the carousel to the account's carousel average.

title: Borrow pacing and camera work from other categories, never the story
hypothesis: If a new format's pacing and camera work is borrowed from a winning video in a different category, but the story and content stay the brand's own, then the account gets a fresh format without copying an already-saturated story.

signal.check: The account needs a new format and has run out of fresh format ideas within its own category.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: Copying the source's story or footage instead of only its structure creates legal and brand risk.

prerequisites: a completed teardown grid on the borrowed format
steps: Pick a winning video from an unrelated category.
Run the teardown grid on its pacing, camera work and structure.
Rebuild the structure with the brand's own product, story and script.
Confirm no text, footage or story element from the source was carried over.

test.method: Compare completion and saves on the new format vs the account baseline.

title: Use next-day recall as a tiebreaker between 2 content concepts
hypothesis: If the team scrolls a batch, waits a day, and notes what it remembers unprompted, then a tie between 2 concepts gets broken by which one is actually memorable, alongside the metric read.

signal.check: The team is stuck choosing between 2 concepts with no clear metric-based winner.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a tiebreaker heuristic, not a measured lift

risk.note: A decision aid only, alongside the metric read.

steps: Scroll the batch of concepts as a normal viewer would.
Return the next day and note what is recalled unprompted.
Use the recall result as a tiebreaker, not a replacement for the metric read.

test.method: Track which concept the recall test favored and whether it also won on metrics.
test.read_point: 1 day after the scroll test, then again after publishing

title: Run a true contrarian angle when category messaging is saturated
hypothesis: If every competitor sells on the same benefit, a true and defensible contrarian angle can find an underserved pocket of buyers instead of adding to the noise.
does_not_apply_when: luxury or regulated categories outside a lower-stakes test account

signal.check: Every competitor's messaging and the store's own posts repeat the same benefit claim and engagement is fatiguing.

expected_effect.size: unknown; hypothetical example, no measured lift

risk.note: A contrarian claim must be true and cleared before publishing to avoid legal or platform risk.

prerequisites: a true, defensible position the brand actually holds
steps: Confirm the category's messaging is genuinely saturated on one benefit.
Find the store's true, underserved angle on the same topic.
Confirm the claim is true, in the brand record, and defensible in the comments.
Run it through the compliance check if it touches health, safety or a competitor.
Publish and do not reject the angle as 'cringe' before testing it.

test.method: Compare engagement and saves on the contrarian post vs the account's category-benefit baseline.

title: Lead the post with the scene closest to the buyer's own life
hypothesis: If the customer scenario opening a post is the one closest to the buyer's own life, place or habit, then it lands better because the viewer already owns or relates to something similar.

signal.check: A post opens with a distant or generic scenario instead of the buyer's own likely context.

expected_effect.size: unknown; single-source example, no measured lift

risk.note: A scene-choice decision only.

steps: List possible opening scenarios for the post.
Pick the one closest to the buyer's actual life, place or habit.
Confirm the scene assumes the viewer already owns or wants something similar.

test.method: Compare hold_rate on proximity-matched scenarios vs generic ones.

title: End every product comparison post with a real, one-sentence verdict
hypothesis: If a versus post states the comparison in the title and gives a professional verdict with reasons, never a hedge, then viewers get a decision they can act on instead of a shrug.

signal.check: A comparison post ('linen vs cotton', 'our pan vs a non-stick') ends with no clear verdict.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: Naming a competitor in a comparison needs a legal review before publishing.

prerequisites: the brand record to back the verdict
steps: State the comparison plainly in the title.
Give a one-sentence verdict backed by the brand record.
Route through legal review if a named competitor is involved.
Cut any hedge that avoids taking a position.

test.method: Compare cvr_overall on comparison posts with a clear verdict vs a hedged ending.

title: Answer the questions buyers are embarrassed to ask
hypothesis: If the education pillar directly answers questions buyers are embarrassed to ask (sizing, care, 'will it tarnish', 'what if it breaks'), then hesitant buyers get the reassurance that comments alone do not surface.

signal.check: Comments repeat hesitant or embarrassed-sounding questions with no post directly addressing them.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: Content planning only.

prerequisites: a month of comments to mine
steps: Pull embarrassed or hesitant-sounding questions from comments.
Pick at least 1 per week starting month 2.
Answer it directly and plainly with the product in hand.

test.method: Compare cvr_overall on posts answering embarrassed questions vs the pillar average.

title: Go deep on the product's subculture to become its reference point
hypothesis: If the account goes obsessively deep on the product's subculture (collectors, hobbyists, trades), then it becomes the reference point for enthusiasts, even though this narrows reach on purpose.
does_not_apply_when: categories with no enthusiast subculture

signal.check: The category has a known enthusiast subculture the account has never spoken to directly.

expected_effect.size: unknown; single-source example, no measured lift

risk.note: A content-focus decision, reversible.

prerequisites: deep product or category knowledge
steps: Identify the enthusiast subculture around the category.
Research the specific details that subculture cares about.
Post content at that level of depth, accepting a smaller but more intense audience.
Track whether the account becomes a cited reference point in that community.

test.method: Track comments and shares from identifiable subculture members over time.
test.read_point: After a quarter of subculture-depth content

title: Sell access to the workshop or sourcing trip, not just the product
hypothesis: If a store with an operation outsiders never see reframes content as a tour of that world instead of a product pitch, then reach and trust grow because the content offers something ordinary product posts do not.
does_not_apply_when: luxury or regulated brands testing raw content, which start on a lower-stakes account

signal.check: A store with a workshop, roastery, supplier or trade-show presence has never shown it in content.

expected_effect.size: one presenter's coffee roaster case reported reach 'expanded significantly' in a couple of weeks; no numbers given

risk.note: A content-angle change only.

prerequisites: access to film the operation
steps: Identify the part of the operation outsiders never see.
Shoot it with travel-documentary energy: raw roasting, packing, staff banter.
Keep the product visible throughout.
Ship at least 1 behind-the-scenes post per pillar cycle.
For luxury or regulated brands, test on a lower-stakes account first.

test.method: Compare reach and saves on behind-the-scenes posts vs the account's studio-content baseline.

title: Reframe a mundane trade show or audit as the event insiders know it is
hypothesis: If a mundane industry date (a trade show, an audit, a seasonal peak) is reframed with an analogy insiders would recognise, then the post earns more attention than a plain calendar update, as long as the analogy survives scrutiny.

signal.check: A trade show, launch, audit or seasonal peak is on the calendar with no planned content angle.

expected_effect.size: unknown; single-source example, no measured lift

risk.note: A framing choice, reversible before publishing.

steps: Identify the mundane industry date on the calendar.
Find an analogy insiders in the category would recognise and respect.
Check the analogy is true enough to survive scrutiny.
Build the post around that reframe.

test.method: Compare reach on reframed event posts vs plain calendar-update posts.

title: Test a first-person founder letter on the PDP and in post-purchase email
hypothesis: If a considered-purchase store tests a plain, first-person founder letter (a contrarian category reframe, a sale, a milestone, an apology) on the PDP and in post-purchase email, then trust may improve, though this is a format to test, not a proven lift.
does_not_apply_when: no willing founder to sign the letter genuinely

signal.check: A considered-purchase store has no founder-voice content on the PDP or in post-purchase flows.

expected_effect.size: unknown; explicitly a format to test, not a proven lift

risk.note: Easy to remove if it underperforms.

prerequisites: a founder willing to sign the letter
a landing page or email flow to place it in (07-LPG, 14-EML)
steps: Draft a contrarian reframe of the category, not the product, as the opener.
Write the letter in plain short sentences, attributable to the named founder.
Place it on the PDP or landing page and in the welcome or post-first-purchase email.
Test it against the current PDP or email copy rather than assuming it wins.

test.method: A/B the founder-letter version against the current PDP or email copy.
test.read_point: After enough traffic for a read, per 09-CRO test design

title: Name a shipping delay or bad batch directly and own it, with no spin
hypothesis: If a shipping delay, recall or bad batch is named directly with what changed and no spin, then the brand keeps trust instead of losing it to a vague or defensive statement.

signal.check: A shipping delay, recall or bad batch has happened and no direct apology post exists yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: A poorly handled apology post cannot be fully undone once seen.

prerequisites: legal review before posting
steps: Name the mistake plainly, with no euphemism.
State exactly what changed to fix it.
Run the post through legal review before publishing.
Avoid defensive or spin language throughout.

test.method: Track comment sentiment and support ticket volume after the apology post.

title: Give away the full how-to; hold back the offer, not the value
hypothesis: If breakdown posts give the full how-to (care, sizing, how it is made) instead of holding some back 'so they buy', then trust builds because most viewers will not execute the how-to themselves and buyers are really buying proof of expertise.

signal.check: A breakdown post holds back real detail because the team fears giving away 'the secret'.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: A content-depth decision only.

steps: Identify what detail is being withheld from a breakdown post.
Give the full breakdown instead.
Keep any hard offer for after traction, not by cutting the content's value.

test.method: Compare saves and comments on full-breakdown posts vs partial ones.

title: Turn verified reviews and customer photos into posts
hypothesis: If a strong review line or a permissioned customer photo is turned into a short post or carousel with the quote as the hook, then the feed shows real customers instead of only brand-made content.

signal.check: The store has a review or UGC pipeline but the feed never shows a customer.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data

risk.note: Confirm permission and verified status before posting.

prerequisites: a review or UGC pipeline with permission tracking
steps: Pull a strong review line or a permissioned customer photo.
Confirm the review's verified status and permission on file.
Build a short post or carousel with the quote as the hook and the product in use as the visual.

test.method: Compare saves and comments on UGC-based posts vs standard brand posts.

title: Put about 80% of new-account effort into product demo Reels, not Stories
hypothesis: If a new account with no followers puts about 80% of effort into product demo and use-case Reels and holds Stories until followers exist, then effort goes where it reaches non-followers, because Stories are seen almost only by existing followers.
does_not_apply_when: accounts that already have a meaningful follower base

signal.check: A new account with no followers is spending meaningful effort on Stories.

expected_effect.size: unknown; single-presenter split, no measured lift

risk.note: A resource-allocation decision only.

steps: Confirm the account has no meaningful follower base yet.
Allocate about 80% of production effort to Reels or short video demos and use cases.
Use carousels for spec comparisons and size or fit guides.
Hold Stories until a follower base exists, then shift Stories to clicks, restocks and CTAs.

test.method: Track non-follower reach after shifting effort to the 80/20 split.
test.read_point: After 4 weeks at the new split

title: Turn a winning format into a named, repeatable series
hypothesis: If a format that beats the rest in the monthly read gets turned into a named, repeatable series instead of a fresh idea each time, then it becomes faster to make and easier for viewers to recognise.
does_not_apply_when: a format with fewer than 4 iterations logged

signal.check: One format has clearly beaten the rest in the monthly read but is still being reinvented as a new idea each time.

expected_effect.size: unknown; several presenters agree on the pattern, no shared number

risk.note: Can be retired if the series underperforms after 4 episodes.

prerequisites: a winner identified from at least 4 iterations in the monthly read
steps: Confirm the format has won across at least 4 iterations.
Give it a name, a fixed visual signature and a promise of what each episode gives.
Set a cadence and commit it to the calendar for at least 8 weeks.
Keep at least 1 other format live alongside it.

test.method: Track the phase metric for the branded series against the account baseline over 8 weeks.
test.read_point: After 8 weeks and every 4 episodes after

title: Give a named series a signature and adapt its length per platform
hypothesis: If a series carries a fixed visual signature and a clear promise of what each episode gives, with length adapted per platform, then viewers can name the series from the first frame and it travels across platforms.

signal.check: A format is about to be branded as a series with no fixed name, visual signature or promise defined yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; single-source example, no measured lift

risk.note: A packaging decision only.

prerequisites: a proven format from the monthly read
steps: Give the series a name and a fixed visual signature.
Write the promise of what each episode gives the viewer.
Adapt the cut length per platform, for example 60 seconds on one platform and longer on another.
Check a viewer can name the series from the first frame alone.

test.method: Ask viewers or the team whether the first frame alone identifies the series.
test.measure: pass rate on the first-frame recognition test

title: Turn a repeatable product demo into a safe, genuine challenge series
hypothesis: If a challenge series is a real stretch, safe, and built as a repeatable product demo (for example 'day N of using the product in a new place'), then it earns attention without needing a dangerous stunt or a trivial daily task.

signal.check: A challenge idea is proposed that is either trivial with no stakes, or requires a dangerous stunt.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: Any stunt-like challenge must be screened for safety before filming.

steps: Define the repeatable demo at the core of the challenge.
Confirm it is a genuine stretch, not trivial and not dangerous.
Check it can be filmed inside the existing batch schedule.
Treat community participation as a bonus, not the design goal.

test.method: Track completion and saves across the challenge's episodes.
test.read_point: After the first week of episodes

title: Prefer formats a team can repeat many times a day without the founder
hypothesis: If new formats are chosen for their ability to be repeated many times in a day without the founder's body, then output can scale past the founder, because a format needing a meal cooked or a trip per episode cannot produce volume.
