title: Add a 90-minute incubation gap between drafting and editing
hypothesis: If a draft sits untouched for at least 90 minutes before editing starts, then the edit catches more real problems, because the writer returns with fresh eyes instead of editing while still attached to the draft's first wording.

signal.check: A script or caption is drafted and edited in the same sitting with no break.

expected_effect.size: unknown; presenter's personal heuristic, no lift given

risk.note: A scheduling change only; delays the piece by under 2 hours.

steps: Finish the dump draft and stop; do not reread it right away.
Step away for at least 90 minutes and do something passive: a walk, a break, another task.
Return and edit hard, cutting and rewriting rather than lightly polishing.
For longer or higher-stakes pieces, extend the gap to a few hours or overnight.

test.method: Compare reviewer-flagged issues on pieces with an incubation gap against pieces edited immediately.
test.read_point: After the next batch of scripts

title: Filter story topics with a 60-second voice-memo test
hypothesis: If a candidate story or topic is recorded as a 60-second voice memo told the way you would tell a friend, then topics that would not naturally come up get dropped before they waste production time, because a forced topic reads as forced on camera too.

signal.check: A topic is added to the content calendar without being tested by saying it out loud informally first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; process claim, no lift given

risk.note: A filtering step only.

steps: Record a 60-second voice memo pitching the topic as if telling a friend.
Listen back and ask whether this would naturally come up in that conversation.
Drop the topic if it feels forced or purely informational.
If it passes, transcribe the memo and lightly edit it into the draft's structure instead of starting from a blank page.

test.method: Track how many voice-memo-filtered topics get finished and published versus topics chosen without the filter.

title: Vary sentence length on purpose in every script and caption
hypothesis: If a script or caption defaults to short sentences and adds a medium or long sentence only after a run of short ones, then the copy reads with rhythm instead of flat monotone, because uniform sentence length is what makes a script feel like a list, not speech.

signal.check: A draft has several sentences in a row of about the same length, or heavy comma use where a period would read better.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: An edit pass only.

steps: Scan the draft for sentences of the same length in a row.
Split any sentence that uses a comma where two short sentences would read cleaner.
After 2 or 3 short sentences, add one medium sentence for pacing.
Add an occasional longer sentence only once the reader has been rested by shorter ones.

test.method: Run a readability and rhythm pass on a sample of scripts before and after the rule is applied.

title: Diagnose stuck copy by explaining it out loud first
hypothesis: If a writer explains a stuck idea out loud in plain speech before rewriting it, then the resulting sentence often becomes the opening line, because copy that will not come out plainly usually means the underlying thinking is not clear yet, not that the wording needs polish.

signal.check: A script, caption or product explanation has been rewritten several times and still reads unclear or corporate.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: A diagnostic step only.

steps: Stop rewriting the stuck line.
Explain the idea out loud to another person, in plain conversational language.
Write down the spoken sentence exactly as said.
Use that sentence as the opening line, or as the copy itself if it already carries the point.
If the idea still cannot be said plainly, treat this as a thinking problem and clarify the idea before rewriting the copy again.

test.method: Compare reviewer notes on copy fixed by the speaking test against copy that got another straight rewrite.

title: Root positioning in a method the store can defend, not a feature list
hypothesis: If the store's positioning names a specific method, process or point of view instead of a feature list, then a competitor cannot copy it in a day, because copying a feature list takes an afternoon while copying reasoning that took years to build takes much longer.

signal.check: The store's positioning statement is a feature or benefit list a competitor's copywriter could paste their own name into and have it still read true.

expected_effect.size: unknown; self-interested example, no lift given

risk.note: A positioning rewrite; test before rolling it into every asset.

prerequisites: a documented process, sourcing method or point of view the brand actually follows
steps: List the specific method, test, sourcing step or stance the store follows that a competitor does not state.
Ask whether a competitor's copywriter could replicate the current positioning in a day without understanding that method.
If yes, rewrite the positioning around the method or reasoning instead of the feature or outcome.
Use the rewritten positioning across the account bio, hooks and PDP intro.

test.method: Ask a small panel whether the new positioning line could belong to a named competitor.
test.read_point: Before rolling the line out everywhere

title: Fund one owned media property instead of another promotion round
hypothesis: If a store puts budget into one recurring owned media property, such as a podcast, video series or newsletter, instead of another round of paid promotion, then it builds a compounding library the store owns, because the content keeps producing new assets long after any single promoted post stops earning attention.

signal.check: The store's content budget only ever buys one-off promoted posts, with nothing recurring or owned.

expected_effect.size: unknown; illustrative example, no lift given

risk.note: A budget reallocation; stop funding it if it produces no reusable material after a defined trial period.

prerequisites: someone able to run the property consistently
a defined budget to reallocate from one-off promotion
steps: Pick one recurring format the store can own: a podcast, a video series or a newsletter.
Name who runs it and how often it publishes.
Route its output into PDP copy, email, ads and social posts instead of judging it only on its own reach.
Set a trial period and a minimum output before judging whether to keep funding it.

test.method: Track how many downstream store assets are mined from the property's output over the trial period.

title: Use a split-screen visual to show a before-and-after comparison
hypothesis: If a comparison claim runs as a split-screen or side-by-side visual instead of a spoken or written comparison, then the difference lands faster, because showing both states at once also acts as a pattern interrupt against the usual single, full-screen video.

signal.check: A before-and-after or old-versus-new claim is only described in words, with no side-by-side visual.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: An editing choice only.

steps: Pick a real before-and-after or old-versus-new comparison the brand record can back.
Film or lay out both states side by side in one frame.
Cut the spoken or written description of the comparison down to a caption, since the visual now carries it.
Test the split-screen version against a described-only version of the same comparison.

test.method: Run the split-screen version against a spoken-comparison version of the same claim.

title: Use a true, time-bound urgency hook tied to a real deadline
hypothesis: If a hook names a specific, true deadline the viewer is about to hit, such as before a restock sells out tonight, then more viewers keep watching for the payoff, because a named moment feels more pressing than a general tip.
does_not_apply_when: no real deadline exists yet, since a fake countdown breaks trust

signal.check: Every hook in the bank is a general tip or fact, with no version tied to a real, immediate moment.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: Only run this on a deadline that is literally true; a fabricated urgency claim is a trust and compliance risk.

prerequisites: a real, verifiable deadline: a restock, a closing window, a real daily habit moment
steps: Confirm a real deadline exists: a restock date, a sale end, a daily routine moment the buyer is actually in.
Write the hook naming that exact moment, not a vague soon.
Check the claim against the brand record before publishing; drop it if the deadline is not literally true.
Tag the hook as urgency type in the hooks bank and log its result.

test.method: Compare hook_rate on urgency-tagged hooks against non-urgency hooks on the same topic.

title: Use a narrow direct-address callout to pull in adjacent viewers
hypothesis: If a hook opens with a narrow, specific callout to one buyer type instead of a broad group, then viewers just outside that group often keep watching to check whether it applies to them too, because a specific callout reads as more credible than a generic one.

signal.check: The hooks bank has no direct-address hook, or its callouts are broad and generic instead of a specific buyer type.

expected_effect.size: unknown; craft claim, no lift given

risk.note: A hook-writing choice only.

steps: Name a specific buyer segment from the brand record, not a broad category.
Open the hook with a direct callout to that segment, such as if you are buying your first one of these, keep watching.
Deliver content that genuinely serves that segment, so adjacent viewers who stay are not misled.
Tag the hook as direct address in the hooks bank and log its result.

test.method: Compare hook_rate and non-follower reach on direct-address hooks against untargeted hooks on the same topic.

title: Choose story subjects for geographic or social proximity
hypothesis: If a story features a real, nearby or identifiable subject, such as a local customer or a named local event, instead of a distant or generic one, then it spreads further by word of mouth, because people repeat stories about things close to them and forget distant ones.

signal.check: Recent stories feature only generic or distant examples, with no locally identifiable customer, place or event.

expected_effect.size: unknown; single-presenter observation, no lift given

risk.note: Get consent before naming a real local customer or business.

prerequisites: a real local customer, event or place with permission to feature it
steps: Find a real, nearby or identifiable customer, event or place tied to the product.
Get permission to name or show it.
Tell the story around that specific, near subject instead of a generic or distant example.
Track whether the post gets more shares or comments referencing the local detail.

test.method: Compare shares and comments on proximity-based stories against generic-subject stories.
test.read_point: After the next few story posts

title: Run 30 to 50 same-topic posts before judging if the platform learned the audience
hypothesis: If the account posts 30 to 50 consecutive pieces on the same topic and avatar before judging reach, then the read on whether the platform has learned the audience is fair, because a post-count threshold catches slow accounts that post the same topic for only a few weeks, which a pure time-based window can miss.

signal.check: The team judges topic targeting as failed after fewer than 30 consecutive same-topic, same-avatar posts.

expected_effect.size: unknown; presenter's own heuristic, not a platform figure

risk.note: A patience rule only; does not block posting anything else.

prerequisites: a single topic and avatar already chosen
steps: Confirm the account is running one topic for one avatar.
Count consecutive posts on that exact topic and avatar.
Hold any targeting verdict until at least 30 posts, and prefer waiting to 50.
State the topic and avatar in both speech and caption on every post in the run, since the count only works if the signal is clean.

test.method: Compare non-follower share of views before post 30 against after post 50 on the same topic run.
test.read_point: At post 30 and again at post 50

title: Repost a timeless post again once it passes 60 days old
hypothesis: If a timeless post is reposted once it is more than 60 days old, then the account gets a second, low-cost pass at reach from the same asset, because a repost reaches a new set of viewers even when the first run was never confirmed as a sales winner.
does_not_apply_when: timely posts tied to a date, launch or trend, which should not be resurfaced

signal.check: Timeless posts sit unrepeated in the archive past 60 days with no repost scheduled.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a single, unexplained line in one source, no mechanism given

risk.note: This rule is thin: the source gives it with no explanation or supporting number, so treat it as a cheap test, not a settled practice.

prerequisites: posts already labelled timely or timeless
steps: Filter the archive for timeless posts older than 60 days.
Repost one as-is or with a light refresh.
Track whether the repost earns meaningful new reach or sales.
Stop the practice if reposts consistently underperform new content.

test.method: Compare reach and sales on 60-day reposts against freshly made posts on the same topic.

title: Reverse-engineer top niche videos with AI before remaking your own
hypothesis: If the top-performing videos in the store's niche are downloaded, transcribed and run through an AI hook-and-pacing checklist before a remake, then the remake starts from evidence of what already works instead of a blank page, because pattern-matching against real winners is a different input than reviewing only your own draft.

signal.check: New scripts are written from a blank page or from memory, with no review of transcribed top-performing niche videos.

expected_effect.size: unknown; single anonymized anecdote reporting a large jump, not a repeatable benchmark

risk.note: A research step; treat any reported lift as a hypothesis to confirm with the store's own before-and-after data.

prerequisites: a shortlist of top-performing niche videos to transcribe
steps: Download and transcribe the top-performing videos in the niche, or the account's own past top performers.
Run the transcripts through an AI tool with targeted questions: hook clarity, comprehension, pacing and drop-off points.
Remake or reshoot the planned content with the suggested changes applied, rather than starting from a blank page.
Confirm any resulting lift with the store's own before-and-after data before treating it as proven.

test.method: Compare hook_rate on AI-reverse-engineered remakes against blank-page scripts on the same topic.
test.read_point: After the next batch of remakes

title: Turn the business's own core skill into an unrelated, impressive demo
hypothesis: If the business's own core skill is applied to something impressive and unrelated to the usual product use, then the skill itself becomes the story people share, because an unexpected demonstration of real competence stops the scroll on its own, without needing the product itself to be dramatic.

signal.check: All content demonstrates the product directly, with no video showing the underlying skill or craft doing something unrelated but impressive.

expected_effect.size: unknown; single anecdotal example, no lift given

risk.note: A one-off production test; keep the core catalogue content running alongside it.

prerequisites: a genuine skill or craft the team can demonstrate on camera
steps: Name the core skill behind the product or service, separate from the product itself.
Pick a surprising, unrelated use for that skill that would impress a stranger.
Film a short demo of the skill in that unrelated context.
Tie it back to the brand only at the end, so the skill carries the hook.

test.method: Compare hook_rate and shares on the skill-demo video against standard product-demo content.
